prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B013 as the whole prize, to Katori and Ye, and I have not changed my configuration since round 1. The chair asks what separates the lattice clock from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. The comb (Hall, Hansch) is a tool for counting optical cycles; the 2012 ion work gave a single, well isolated absorber whose uncertainty is bought by having one quantum system. The lattice clock is neither. Its content is the magic-wavelength condition: choose the trap wavelength so that the differential light shift of the clock transition vanishes, which lets one confine thousands of neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime without the Stark and Doppler penalties. The practical consequence is what I as an experimentalist care about most: the statistical signal-to-noise of many atoms, so that a 1e-18 systematic evaluation can be reached in hours of averaging and not weeks or months. That is why the clock comparisons between laboratories became possible at that level at all. A citation written around magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms does not read as a third clock prize, because it names a mechanism that neither earlier prize contains. On evidence, the 1e-18 figure rests on blackbody-radiation, lattice-light and density-shift characterisation that has been cross-checked by independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, including fibre-linked comparisons, so the maturity question is answered by data and not by projection. I would not wait for the redefinition of the second: that is a metrological decision by a different body, and the physics was demonstrated years ago.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection is real and I cannot dismiss it entirely. Ion clocks reached the low 1e-17 systematic range around 2010, so the claim that the lattice clock simply is the first at 1e-18 is weaker than the claim that it is the first to combine that accuracy with many-atom stability, and the citation should say the latter. The committee may also still feel that this is outstanding measurement science without an unexpected result about nature: no varying constant or dark-sector signal has come out of the clocks, only limits and a relativistic geodesy demonstration. I regard limits and a millimetre-scale gravitational-redshift measurement as delivered physics, but I accept that reasonable members weigh it differently. Credit is the third concern. Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde, Hollberg and the ion-clock groups all contributed, and a two-name prize leaves them out. I have no documentary evidence, only my knowledge of the field, that would move a third name onto the list, and I would support an expert check on the 2001-2003 priority record before the vote.

responses.point: She argues that the clock is precision atomic-structure physics in which theory and experiment must agree in every detail, but also grants that the committee may read it as metrology and that no fundamental-physics result has yet come out of it. She suggests a two-part prize pairing the clock with B001 might be stronger.
responses.response: I agree with her framing of the risk and I think her citation, which names tests of fundamental physics, is a sensible hedge. On the pairing with B001 I would not do it. B013 is complete as a single achievement with two cleanly separable laureates, and adding a second part would force the committee to settle the Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller and Cirac credit question under a three-person cap without any member preferring B001 in round 1. The cap would also mean trimming Katori or Ye or the quantum-simulation group. If the committee later wants B001 it deserves its own year. On her point that blackbody and lattice-shift evaluations matter more than structure theory, the black-body shift is exactly where atomic theory and experiment had to be reconciled, so we are not far apart.

responses.point: As chair he supports B013 but says he would want expert input on the relative priority of Katori, Ye and the earlier lattice-clock proposals, and notes that ion-clock and Yb or Al+ groups traded the accuracy record.
responses.response: I agree that an external priority check is prudent given that none of us, including me, is working from verified documents. On the record-trading point I want to be exact: the Al+ ion clock did reach a lower systematic uncertainty than the first neutral-atom clocks around 2010, so the citation should not claim the lowest uncertainty in absolute terms. What the lattice clock brought was the combination of 1e-18 accuracy with the stability of many atoms, and I would phrase the citation around that. I would also push back gently on any suggestion that the chair's non-specialist status weakens the case. The decision rests on cross-laboratory reproducibility, which a non-specialist can assess. I withdraw nothing from my round-1 view of B035: IceCube is a serious alternative, but source identification still rests on a few objects and the credit is split among collaboration leaders.

responses.point: He keeps B048 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) first as a new state of matter with a stable interpretation, but concedes the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit and the 3D topological insulator work cannot be repaired and names B013 as the safer fallback.
responses.response: I take his new-state-of-matter argument seriously, and the HgTe experiment is a beautiful and clean measurement of the predicted edge conductance. I do not think it beats B013 at this stage for the reasons he himself gives. A prize that must exclude the person who proposed HgTe as the host, and cannot reach the 3D case, would be defended after the fact, and the 2016 prize leaves the question of what is new open. He asks whether strong consensus for the clock should override his preference for a new state of matter. I do not think consensus should override scientific judgment, and I would not ask him to move because the others have. But I would ask him to weigh that his own text calls B013 the safer choice for the same attribution reasons that make me prefer it. If he can write a three-name B048 citation that survives the Zhang objection, I would read it with interest.

responses.point: She moved from B050 to B013, noting that the optical comb is a necessary technical foundation for any optical clock, so the lattice-clock contribution must be shown to be distinct from the 2005 prize.
responses.response: Her observation is right and I should have conceded it more directly in round 1: every optical clock needs a comb to count the cycles, so the comb is infrastructure for B013, not a part of it. The distinction I draw is between the counting tool, honoured in 2005, and the choice of trapped system and trapping condition, which is what Katori contributed. I also note that she moved after reading the other ballots, as did several of us. I would treat that convergence cautiously, and I think the right test is whether the reasons survive, not the count. The reasons I find robust are reproducibility, a mechanism that is separate from the comb and the ion work, and clean two-person credit. Her reservation about recalling priority from memory is the same as mine, so I support the expert check.

uncertainties: Whether the citation can be worded so that it names magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms and the many-atom stability gain, and so does not imply a third prize for clocks in general after 2005 and 2012.
Whether the historical priority record (Katori 2001-2003, Ye and JILA, other early lattice-clock proposals) supports exactly Katori and Ye, which none of us has checked against documents.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second or for a first delivered fundamental-physics result such as a constants or dark-sector limit from the clocks.
Whether a majority that formed after reading each other's ballots reflects independent judgment, which is why I stress that the reasons, not the count, justify B013.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has appeared in the discussion and none is requested. As a Lund atomic physicist I know the cold-atom and optical-clock communities professionally, and my profile shows a stay in John Hall's lab during my PhD, but Hall is not a candidate and Katori and Ye are not collaborators or co-authors of mine. My WACQT role overlaps with Johansson's institution, which would matter only for circuit QED (B008), which I ranked fifth and do not now support. I have no commercial interest in any shortlisted candidate; my company works on ultrasound optical tomography.
